newsitem.title: INDIA: India's defeated Deve Gowda promises to rise again.
newsitem.headline: India's defeated Deve Gowda promises to rise again.

text.p: Ousted in a lop-sided vote of confidence earlier this month, former Indian prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda promised on Wednesday to rise again to lead his embattled centre-left coalition to a more secure future.
"I will rise from the dust," the 64-year old leader told reporters at a luncheon he hosted at the prime minister's official residence in New Delhi.
He will vacate the heavily fortified house this week for his successor, Inder Kumar Gujral, who won a vote of confidence on the same floor of parliament late on Tuesday.

"I have enjoyed the 10 months of my job thoroughly, as anyone who longs to serve the country should," he said, shepherding journalists around the sprawling colonial-style bungalow, his arms resting around the shoulders of some.

Deve Gowda showed no signs of bitterness over his defeat on April 11, when his ally-turned-foe, the Congress party, joined hands with the rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to hand him a crushing defeat in the trust vote.
The final official tally was 338 votes against Deve Gowda, 190 for and four abstentions.
"For 10 months I was aware of the sword hanging over my head," Deve Gowda recalled. "I knew I had very little time so I plunged into my job headlong.
"It was not easy to keep a coalition of 14 totally different kind of groups together. It was a big challenge," he said.
Asked if the same sword hung over his successor's head, Deve Gowda said: "I do not want to comment on that, you should ask him. But I am feeling very peaceful at the moment. I needed the rest."
Indian businessmen had hailed Deve Gowda's 10 month-rule as an impressive pro-reform regime despite having to manage the country's largest collection of disparate political groups ever.
But Deve Gowda said his most important task was to keep the country together, emphasising its federal character.

"No prime minister had visited all the Indian states in 10 months. I have, including four visits to Jammu and Kashmir," he said, referring to the troubled Himalayan region where his government staged the first state polls in seven years.

"Knowing the problems of the country first hand was rewarding," said Deve Gowda, who has frequently admitted to having a limited notion of India when he was chief minister of the southern state of Karnataka before his surprise elevation last June.
He was the third choice of the United Front, a coalition of communists, free-market ideologues, regional and low-caste Hindu satraps, cobbled together after inconclusive polls last May.
Former Indian prime minister Vishwanath Pratap Singh and Jyoti Basu, the communist Chief Minister of the state of West Bengal, had earlier turned down the job.
"It was my destiny, nothing else," Deve Gowda said, repeating a refrain that has characterised his popular image as a humble farmer.

Congress president Sitaram Kesri withdrew support for Deve Gowda, accusing him of sidelining the party. Gujral has set up a coordination committee headed by himself and Kesri to sort out any policy differences to avoid a future collision.
"I am not going to be a part of that committee. I don't want to interefere with the government," said Deve Gowda, who remains the chairman of the United Front.
